title: Why Small Talk May Be Killing Your Opportunities
author: Vanessa Van Edwards
summary: In this guest post on Nir Eyal’s newsletter, Vanessa Van Edwards argues that small talk is a learnable skill and that mediocre small talk is costly because conversations end before anything meaningful begins. She draws on research by Kardas, Kumar and Epley showing that people overestimate how awkward deeper conversations will feel, and on Boothby’s liking gap, to explain why we default to shallow topics. Her Conversation Blueprint moves from putting people at ease to uncovering goals and then to understanding someone’s story, and she frames the effort as a treasure hunt using question swaps. She also advises replacing vague answers to "What do you do?" with a short logline in the form "I [do what] for [who] by [how]." Her closing practice is to ask about goals, respond as a dreambuilder rather than a dreamkiller, share your own goals, look for ways to help and check in later. The piece is practical interpersonal-skills guidance for anyone who needs to build relationships at work.
points: People consistently predict that deeper conversations with strangers will feel awkward but report feeling happier and more connected after having them, so the safe shallow choice is usually the wrong one.
Small talk works best as the first of three levels that move a stranger toward an ally: put people at ease, uncover goals and challenges, then understand their story.
A one-sentence logline of the form "I do what for who by how" gives the other person an easy next question, whereas vague purpose statements give them nothing to attach to.
Asking "What’s your biggest goal right now?" signals care and points the conversation toward the other person’s desired future.
Responding to someone’s goal with curiosity ("Tell me more") instead of fact-checking, and then following up later, is the habit that most deepens relationships.
quotes: Engaging, memorable conversations can open doors. We hire, recommend, promote, and want to spend time with people who are likable and easy to talk to.
You think the other person likes you less than they actually do, and you think going deeper will make the interaction more awkward than it actually will.
That’s why mediocre small talk can be so costly. Nothing obviously bad happens. The conversation simply ends before anything meaningful has a chance to begin.
The mistake is thinking you need to jump straight from “How’s the weather?” to “Tell me about your childhood trauma.
I call this the Hierarchy of Facts. People need to understand your what before they can make sense of your why.
You know your logline is working when the other person gives you somewhere to go next:
Dreambuilding does not mean you have to agree with everything someone says. It means you get curious before you get critical.
Reciprocal disclosure turns a conversation into a relationship instead of an interview.
The best conversationalists I know don’t dominate conversations. They create better ones.
